references.text: The parallel account in [ref:Matt 26:57|Matthew 26:57] tells how Jesus was brought to the high priest Caiaphas after his arrest. Matthew mentions the high priest by name, while Luke leaves it unnamed.
[ref:Mark 14:53|Mark 14:53] is the closest parallel in the Gospel of Mark, where Jesus is brought to the high priest and all the chief priests, elders, and scribes gather.
In [ref:Joh 18:13-14|John 18:13–14], Jesus is first taken to Annas, the father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas. John gives a more detailed picture of the sequence of events than Luke does.
[ref:Joh 18:24|John 18:24] tells that Annas sent Jesus bound to the high priest Caiaphas, which complements Luke's account that Jesus was brought into the high priest's house.
In [ref:Luk 22:33|Luke 22:33], Peter had declared he was willing to go to prison and to death with Jesus. Now he follows at a distance, showing the beginning of his failure.

[ref:Matt 26:58|Matthew 26:58] is the parallel that describes how Peter followed Jesus at a distance all the way into the high priest's courtyard, where he sat among the guards to see what would happen.
[ref:Mark 14:54|Mark 14:54] reports that Peter followed Jesus at a distance, all the way into the high priest's courtyard, where he sat with the guards and warmed himself by the fire.
[ref:Joh 18:15-16|John 18:15–16] gives more details about how Peter entered the high priest's courtyard: another disciple who knew the high priest helped Peter get in.

The arrest described here in verse 54 is the result of plans made in [ref:Luk 22:3-4|Luke 22:3–4], where Satan entered Judas, who went to the chief priests and temple guards to arrange how he could betray Jesus.

[ref:Sal 31:12|Psalm 31:12] expresses the complaint of the suffering righteous one about being abandoned by friends and acquaintances: "I have become a scorn for all my enemies." Peter's following at a distance reflects this loneliness.

[ref:Jes 53:7|Isaiah 53:7] prophesies about the suffering servant who was mistreated but did not open his mouth—a prophecy fulfilled as Jesus willingly allows himself to be led to the high priest's house without resistance.
